objectives.text: Distinguish EMR, EMT, AEMT and Paramedic by scope, and state what AEMT adds
objectives.enables: Know before you act whether a skill is yours to perform or one you must call for

objectives.text: Differentiate scope of practice, standard of care, protocol, and licensure, certification and credentialing
objectives.enables: Recognise when an instruction you have been given would take you outside your scope

objectives.text: Identify the components of an EMS system and how a call moves through them
objectives.enables: Know who to ask for what when something on a call is not going to plan

objectives.text: Differentiate online from offline medical direction and apply standing orders
objectives.enables: Act on a standing order without delay, and know the point at which you must call

objectives.text: Apply destination logic using specialty centre capability and transfer requirements
objectives.enables: Choose a destination that can actually treat the problem, rather than the nearest door

objectives.text: Explain continuous quality improvement and how evidence changes practice
objectives.enables: Read a practice change and judge what it rests on, instead of taking it on authority

objectives.text: Describe professional attributes and define mobile integrated healthcare
objectives.enables: Recognise the conduct that keeps a licence, and what MIH asks of a crew

objectives.text: Integrate scope, medical direction and destination on a single call
objectives.enables: Hold all three together under time pressure, which is when they conflict

blocks.title: What an AEMT actually is

cold_open.text: Your first shift. The crew chief says the truck is running "AEMT tonight, no medic". Your partner is an EMT. Somewhere between what the two of you can do and what a paramedic could do, there is a line, and by the end of the shift you will have stood on it at least once.

screens.body_md:
**Four levels, and each one contains the one below it.** Emergency Medical Responder, EMT, Advanced EMT, Paramedic.

A paramedic has not stopped being able to do EMT things. The scopes are cumulative, which is why a mixed crew works and why the highest level present sets the ceiling for the call.

**EMR** is designed for someone who arrives before an ambulance: compressions, an AED, bleeding control, an airway held open. Minimal equipment, immediate actions.

**EMT** adds a fuller assessment, oxygen, a small set of medications mostly by simple routes, splinting and extrication.

What the EMT level does not include is anything that enters a vein or breaks the skin, and that single boundary is where your own new scope begins.

**AEMT is where access begins.** The defining additions are intravenous access, a wider set of medications and routes, and advanced airway adjuncts short of intubation.

The pattern is worth naming: AEMT adds *access and a limited drug set*. It does not add independent diagnosis, and it does not add invasive procedures.

**Paramedic** adds rhythm interpretation and manual defibrillation, intubation, needle decompression, and a much larger formulary.

The clinical consequence for you is simple: when a patient needs one of those, the useful question is not whether you could attempt it, but how quickly someone who is licensed for it can get there.

**Nobody on scene can move that line.** Not a paramedic partner, not a physician on the radio, not the urgency of the patient.

That sounds obvious written down. It is much less obvious at 0300 with a sick patient and a colleague telling you to get on with it — which is why it is worth deciding now, calmly, what you will say.

blocks.callback_md:
The line runs between access and interpretation. You can start an IV and give what your protocol authorises through it; you cannot interpret a rhythm and shock on your own reading, and you cannot intubate.

**And the line does not move.** Not for a partner, not for a physician, not for how sick the patient is. That last part is the whole of the answer.

blocks.title: Scope, protocol, licensure

cold_open.text: A colleague at another service tells you they give a drug you have never been allowed to give. Same certification, same state, same national standard. Either one of you is doing something wrong, or the words you are both using do not mean quite what you think they mean.

screens.body_md:
**Scope of practice is a legal ceiling**, set by your state. It is the complete list of things someone at your level may ever do there.

It is a ceiling and not a checklist. Being within scope means you *may*, not that you *should*, and not that you are authorised today.

**Protocol is your medical director’s written instruction**, and it sits inside the scope.

A protocol can be narrower than your scope and frequently is. It cannot be wider: no medical director can authorise a skill your licence does not include.

You practise in the overlap of the two, and the overlap is always the smaller circle.

**Three words get confused constantly.**

**Certification** says a national body examined you and you passed.
**Licensure** says a state permits you to practise there.
**Credentialing** says one employer permits you to practise for them.

Certification travels with you. The other two do not. That is why moving states means starting two of the three again.

**Standard of care is none of these.** It is how your conduct is judged afterwards: what a reasonable provider of the same level would have done, in the same circumstances.

Not the best provider. Not with hindsight. Protocol is strong evidence of what reasonable looks like, which is why departing from it needs a reason you can state out loud.

**This is the block worth knowing cold.** Scope confusion is the most common root of disciplinary action at this level, and the reason is structural: nothing on scene stops you.

No alarm sounds when you cross the line. It is found afterwards, in a review, by someone reading your chart — and by then the act is already done.

blocks.callback_md:
Neither of you is necessarily wrong. **Scope is set by the state; protocol is set by your medical director inside it.** Two services in one state can hold identical scope and different protocols, and both be practising correctly.

What you cannot conclude is that because they may, you may. Your authority comes from your protocol, not from their practice.

*Kansas AEMT scope and the AMR KC standing orders belong here as a local layer. They have not been added to this module yet.*

blocks.title: How the system is built

cold_open.text: By the time you pull up, a neighbour has already called, a dispatcher has already triaged the call and talked someone through compressions, and a first responder has already put hands on the chest. Three things have gone right before you have done anything at all.
cold_open.decision_point: What else is holding this call up that you cannot see?

screens.body_md:
**A system is what exists between calls.** Any single call runs through it: someone recognises an emergency and calls, dispatch triages and sends, a crew assesses and treats, the patient is transported, care is handed over.

Every one of those is a link, and the chain is only as good as its weakest.

**Public access and dispatch do more than send a truck.** Emergency medical dispatch triages the call, sends the right resource, and gives pre-arrival instructions.

Bystander compressions and early bleeding control started on the phone are among the highest-value interventions in the entire system — higher than most of what happens after you arrive.

**Medical direction is present on every call**, whether or not you speak to anybody. Your protocols are a physician’s judgement, written down in advance.

**Transport and destination** are part of the system too. Which facilities exist, what they can do, and where a patient is taken were decided long before your shift started.

**Two components look backward rather than forward.**

**Continuous quality improvement** reviews what was done and feeds it into what is taught next. **Public education and prevention** reduces the number of calls that happen at all.

Neither helps the patient in front of you. Both decide what the next hundred patients get.

**Why this matters on a bad call:** when something is not going to plan, the useful question is which part of the system owns the problem.

No crew available is a deployment question. No capable hospital within reach is a system-design question. Neither is solved by the two of you driving faster, and both are solved by someone — if they are told.

blocks.callback_md:
Medical direction, written before you arrived. A destination plan that decided which hospitals could take this patient. A deployment model that put your truck where it was. A CQI process that will look at this call next month.

None of it is visible on scene, and all of it is holding the call up. **When a call is failing for reasons you cannot fix with your hands, it is usually one of these — and they change only if someone says so.**

blocks.title: Medical direction

cold_open.text: Wheezing, tight, frightened, and your protocol has a standing order for a nebulised bronchodilator that fits this patient exactly. Your partner reaches for the radio to ask medical control for permission. The drug is in your hand.
cold_open.decision_point: Do you wait for the radio?

screens.body_md:
**Every prehospital intervention happens under a physician’s authority.** Yours comes in two forms.

**Offline** direction is written in advance: your protocols and standing orders.
**Online** direction is contemporaneous contact with a physician about this patient, now.

Most of a shift runs on offline direction, and you may never use the other.

**A standing order is a decision already made.** The physician considered this presentation in advance and wrote down what to do.

When the presentation matches, you act. Calling to ask permission for something already permitted spends exactly the minutes the standing order was written to save, and returns no new information.

The physician who wrote it judged that the delay of a call would cost the patient more than it gained. Waiting anyway quietly overrides that judgement, without anyone deciding to.

**Call when the written direction runs out.** Three occasions:

The presentation fits no standing order you hold. You believe a departure from protocol is in the patient’s interest. Or the protocol itself tells you to call.

That is the whole test: *does written direction already cover this, exactly?* If yes, act. If no, call.

**An order you cannot lawfully perform is still an order you decline.** A physician cannot extend your licence, any more than a paramedic partner can.

Say what you cannot do and offer what you can. It is uncomfortable once and defensible forever, and it is rare enough that it is worth rehearsing before it happens.

**Read every radio order back.** Repeat it, have it confirmed, then act.

A misheard drug or a misheard dose is caught at exactly one moment, and that moment is before you give it. The read-back costs about four seconds and it is the only step in the chain that catches the error.

It also puts the order in your partner’s hearing, which gives a wrong dose a second person who might notice it.

blocks.callback_md:
**No.** The standing order is medical direction, already given, for exactly this presentation. Give the drug.

The radio is for when the written direction runs out — when nothing covers the patient, when you want to depart from what does, or when the protocol tells you to call. None of those is true here, and the patient is short of breath while you wait.

blocks.title: Where the patient goes

cold_open.text: Two hospitals. One is twenty minutes away and can admit almost anything. The other is fifty minutes away and is the only one within reach that can do the procedure your patient needs tonight. Your patient is stable enough to make the journey, and does not much want to.
cold_open.decision_point: Which way do you turn out of the driveway?

screens.body_md:
**Nearest is a default, not a rule.** It is the right answer when the patient will not survive the extra distance, and only then.

The real question is never which door is closest. It is which route reaches the *definitive treatment* soonest — and for some conditions the nearest door cannot provide it at all.

**Specialty systems exist because some treatments are time-dependent and not universal.** Trauma centres, stroke centres, cardiac and PCI centres, burn and paediatric centres.

Taking a patient to a facility that must then stabilise and transfer them costs two journeys and the wait in between, which almost always exceeds the longer first transport.

**Interfacility transfers are destination decisions made by someone else.** The sending clinician specifies the level of care the patient needs in transit, and the service must meet it.

Accepting a transfer above your level is a scope problem that starts before the wheels move, and it is much harder to fix once you are on the road.

**Patient preference is real and it has limits.** Continuity of care at a hospital that holds their records is a genuine clinical benefit.

The tighter the clinical time pressure, the less room there is. In a stable patient there is usually room; in a time-critical one there is often none, and saying so plainly is better than deciding silently.

**Where protocol directs a destination, it governs.** Most disputes dissolve once someone explains the reason rather than asserting the rule.

The ones that do not are what medical control is for. A contested destination is a legitimate reason to pick up the radio.

Name the protocol, name the capability the patient needs, and offer the radio. That sequence settles most disputes before anybody has to be overruled.

blocks.callback_md:
Toward the procedure — assuming your protocol directs it and he remains stable enough for the journey. The nearer hospital would have to stabilise and transfer him anyway, and that costs him more time than the extra thirty minutes does.

**But tell him why.** A patient who understands that the closer hospital cannot do the thing he needs is usually no longer arguing, and a patient who is simply overruled complains later — reasonably.

blocks.title: Quality, safety and evidence

cold_open.text: An instructor tells you a technique is standard because it has been taught that way for thirty years. Later the same week you read that a large review found no evidence it helps, and some evidence it harms. Both statements are true at once.
cold_open.decision_point: Which one should change what you do?

screens.body_md:
**Continuous quality improvement looks for causes, not culprits.** It reviews care across many calls to find the pattern behind a problem, and then changes the system.

A review process people are afraid of stops being told things. Once that happens it is worse than having none, because it produces reassuring reports about a service that is not actually safe.

**The near miss is the cheapest information a system ever gets.** An error that harmed nobody tells you a hole exists, at no cost to a patient.

Report it. The alternative is waiting for the same hole to be found by someone who is harmed by it, which is how most systems actually learn and is a terrible way to do it.

**Longevity is not evidence.** A practice taught for thirty years has been taught for thirty years. That is all it establishes.

Several long-standing EMS practices have turned out to lack evidence of benefit, and a few carried harm. They persisted because they were taught, not because they worked.

**Three questions separate an improvement from a fashion.**

What evidence supports it, and how strong is it? What outcome was actually measured — survival, or a number on a monitor? And who benefits if this is adopted?

The third is not cynicism. It is simply worth knowing when a product is involved.

**You will meet this again in this series.** Two practices ahead of you are taught by the textbook and not supported by current evidence, and the module will show you the book position and the evidence side by side.

That is deliberate. Being able to say "here is what the book says, here is what the evidence says" is itself part of practising at this level.

blocks.callback_md:
The review should — but through your medical director, not by you unilaterally on the next call. Protocol is theirs, and appraising evidence against current practice is exactly what that role is for.

**What the thirty years establishes is that it has been taught for thirty years.** Nothing more. Holding both facts at once, without resolving them by deferring to whoever spoke last, is the skill this block is teaching.

blocks.title: Professionalism and MIH

cold_open.text: Same address, fourth time this month. Nothing is ever badly wrong. Your partner has stopped bothering to take a full history, and the patient has stopped expecting one. Everyone in the room has quietly agreed this call does not really count.
cold_open.decision_point: What has gone wrong here, and whose problem is it?

screens.body_md:
**Professional attributes are not decoration.** Integrity, respect, self-motivation, appearance and manner, and careful communication appear in every professional standard, and each has a clinical reason.

Integrity is why the record can be relied on. Respect is why the patient tells you things. Self-motivation is why a rarely used skill still works when you need it.

**Trust is an assessment tool.** History is the larger part of your assessment, and it depends entirely on being told the truth.

A frightened or unconvinced patient tells you less, so you decide with less. That is why manner is treated as clinical rather than cosmetic — it changes the quality of your data.

**Skills decay whether or not anyone checks.** The ones you rarely use decay fastest, and pressure is exactly when that shows.

Saying "I have not done this in a year and I want to refresh it" is the professional act. Reading a procedure for the first time at a bedside is not competence, and everyone present can tell.

**Mobile integrated healthcare treats EMS as a healthcare resource that happens to be mobile.** Follow-up visits, assessment at home, help navigating to the service that actually meets the need.

Measured by needs met rather than patients moved, and often the answer to a person who keeps calling because nothing else has worked.

It is not a scope change and not a new certification. It is the same providers, sent against a different question.

**A frequent caller is usually a signal.** Repeated use of an emergency service is a healthcare problem with a healthcare answer, not a character defect and not something to be endured.

It is also the clearest example of why 1.3 mattered: the fix is almost never on the truck, and the people who can fix it only find out if somebody tells them.

blocks.callback_md:
The assessment has quietly stopped happening, which means the day something *is* badly wrong, nobody will notice. Familiarity has become a clinical risk.

**And the repeat calls themselves are the signal.** Four visits in a month is a need being met nowhere else — which is a system problem, with a system answer, that will keep recurring until somebody names it.

blocks.title: Integration — scope, direction and destination

cold_open.text: Everything in this chapter arrives on the same call, usually in the wrong order and usually at night. Scope, medical direction and destination do not take turns. They land together, and each one changes what the others allow you to do.
cold_open.decision_point: Can you hold all three at once?

screens.body_md:
**Three questions, running at the same time.**

What am I licensed and authorised to do? Who is directing this care, and does the written direction already cover it? And where does this patient need to end up?

What follows is one call. Each question comes up more than once, and at least one of the answers changes partway through.

blocks.callback_md:
Aspirin on the standing order, without calling. The PCI centre, because the nearer hospital cannot do the thing he needs. A diversion when his airway failed, because capability stops winning the moment the patient will not survive the distance. And a declined order, because nobody on a radio can widen your licence.

Four decisions, all defensible, and the reasons are different in each case. **That is what holding all three at once actually looks like.**

items.stem: What most clearly distinguishes the AEMT level from the EMT level?

options.text: A limited set of advanced skills, including IV access and selected medications
options.rationale: AEMT adds a defined set of advanced skills on top of the EMT foundation.

options.text: The ability to work without medical direction
options.rationale: Every level works under medical direction. AEMT does not change that.

options.text: Authority to determine a patient’s diagnosis
options.rationale: No prehospital level diagnoses. Providers form impressions and treat findings.

options.text: Supervision of EMTs on scene
options.rationale: Crew roles are set by the agency, not by the certification level.

items.explanation_md: The Scope of Practice Model builds each level on the one below it. AEMT is the EMT scope plus a limited advanced set — not a different kind of practice.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Sort each skill by the lowest level licensed to perform it.

options.text: Automated external defibrillation
options.rationale: AED use is within the EMT scope.

options.text: Peripheral IV access
options.rationale: IV access is one of the skills AEMT adds.

options.text: Cardiac rhythm interpretation and manual defibrillation
options.rationale: Manual defibrillation and rhythm interpretation are paramedic-level.

options.text: Oral glucose for a conscious hypoglycaemic patient
options.rationale: Oral glucose is an EMT skill.

items.explanation_md: Each level includes everything below it. A skill being within your scope is separate from whether your protocol authorises it today.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Which level is the entry point of the national licensure structure?

options.text: Emergency Medical Responder
options.rationale: EMR is the first level, intended for those who arrive before an ambulance.

options.text: Emergency Medical Technician
options.rationale: EMT is the second level, built on EMR.

options.text: Advanced EMT
options.rationale: AEMT is the third level.

options.text: Paramedic
options.rationale: Paramedic is the highest of the four.

items.explanation_md: Four levels: EMR, EMT, AEMT, Paramedic. Each is a superset of the one before it.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Select everything the AEMT level typically adds to the EMT scope.

options.text: Establishing peripheral intravenous access
options.rationale: IV access is a defining AEMT addition.

options.text: Administering a limited set of medications by additional routes
options.rationale: AEMT widens both the drug list and the routes available.

options.text: Supraglottic airway placement
options.rationale: Advanced airway adjuncts short of intubation sit at AEMT.

options.text: Interpreting a 12-lead electrocardiogram
options.rationale: That is paramedic-level.

options.text: Performing needle decompression of the chest
options.rationale: Needle thoracostomy is a paramedic skill.

items.explanation_md: The pattern is access and a limited drug set, not independent diagnosis or invasive procedures.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: A paramedic asks you, an AEMT, to push a drug that is outside your scope while they manage the airway. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, and offer to take over the airway so they can give it
options.rationale: Scope is a legal limit on you. A colleague cannot widen it, and swapping tasks solves the problem.

options.text: Give it, since a paramedic directed you
options.rationale: A verbal instruction does not extend your licence. You would be acting outside scope.

options.text: Give it and document that the paramedic ordered it
options.rationale: Documenting an out-of-scope act does not make it lawful.

options.text: Call medical control for permission
options.rationale: Medical control cannot authorise a skill your licence does not include.

items.explanation_md: Scope is set by the state and is not negotiable on scene. Neither a partner nor a physician can extend it.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: An EMR arrives first at a cardiac arrest. What should you expect them to have done?

options.text: Started compressions and applied an AED
options.rationale: EMR scope covers immediate lifesaving care with minimal equipment.

options.text: Established an IV and given epinephrine
options.rationale: Both are beyond EMR scope.

options.text: Placed a supraglottic airway
options.rationale: Advanced airway adjuncts are above EMR.

options.text: Interpreted the rhythm and defibrillated manually
options.rationale: Manual defibrillation is paramedic-level.

items.explanation_md: EMR exists to close the gap before the ambulance. Knowing what they can do tells you what you are walking into.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Is each skill within the AEMT scope?

rows.label: Intravenous access
Endotracheal intubation
Supraglottic airway
Manual defibrillation
Blood glucose measurement

items.explanation_md: The national model sets the ceiling. Your state may sit below it, and your protocol may sit below that again.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Why does the national model describe levels as building on one another rather than as separate jobs?

options.text: Because every level keeps the whole scope beneath it, so a higher level never loses a lower skill
options.rationale: A paramedic still performs EMT care. The levels are cumulative.

options.text: Because each level replaces the one below it
options.rationale: Nothing is given up on moving up a level.

options.text: Because the levels are interchangeable on scene
options.rationale: They are not. Each has a defined ceiling.

options.text: Because states are required to license all four
options.rationale: States decide which levels they license.

items.explanation_md: Cumulative scope is why a crew of mixed levels works: the higher level can do everything the lower one can, and more.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Which of these is set by the state rather than by your employer or medical director?

options.text: Scope of practice
options.rationale: Scope is defined in state law and regulation.

options.text: Protocol
options.rationale: Protocol is written by the medical director, inside the state scope.

options.text: Credentialing
options.rationale: Credentialing is an agency verifying an individual may practise there.

options.text: Shift assignment
options.rationale: An operational matter, not a legal one.

items.explanation_md: Scope comes from the state. Protocol narrows it. Credentialing decides which individuals may work under it.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Sort each statement by which concept it describes.

options.text: The skills state law permits at your level
options.rationale: That is the definition of scope.

options.text: What a reasonable provider of your level would do in the same situation
options.rationale: That is the standard of care, and it is a negligence concept.

options.text: Your medical director’s written instruction for a presentation
options.rationale: That is protocol.

options.text: The legal ceiling on what you may perform at all
options.rationale: Also scope — it is a ceiling, not a checklist.

items.explanation_md: Scope is a legal ceiling. Protocol is an instruction inside it. Standard of care is how your conduct is judged afterwards.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A skill is within your state scope but your agency protocol does not include it. May you perform it?

options.text: No — protocol may narrow scope, and you practise under your protocol
options.rationale: You may do what is in both. Protocol narrowing scope is normal and binding.

options.text: Yes — state scope overrides agency protocol
options.rationale: Scope permits; it does not require. Your medical director decides what you actually do.

options.text: Yes, if a paramedic agrees
options.rationale: A colleague cannot authorise you outside your protocol.

options.text: Only if you document the reason
options.rationale: Documentation does not authorise an act.

items.explanation_md: Think of it as two circles. You practise in the overlap, and the overlap is always the smaller of the two.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Who confers each of these?

rows.label: Licensure to practise
Certification of competence by examination
Credentialing to work at this service

items.explanation_md: Certification says you passed. Licensure says the state permits you. Credentialing says this employer permits you. All three are needed.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: You move to another state holding a current national certification. What do you still need?

options.text: A licence from the new state, and credentialing by the new employer
options.rationale: Certification travels; the authority to practise does not.

options.text: Nothing — national certification is a licence
options.rationale: It is evidence of competence, not permission to practise.

options.text: Only employer credentialing
options.rationale: The state must license you as well.

options.text: Only a state licence
options.rationale: The employer must still credential you.

items.explanation_md: This is the practical reason the three words are not interchangeable, and why the distinction is worth holding.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select every situation that puts you outside your scope of practice.

options.text: Performing a skill your licence level does not include
options.rationale: That is the definition of exceeding scope.

options.text: Performing a skill after your licence has lapsed
options.rationale: Without a current licence you have no scope at all.

options.text: Performing a skill a physician verbally asked you to do that is above your level
options.rationale: A physician cannot extend a licence.

options.text: Performing a skill in your scope that your protocol omits
options.rationale: That is a protocol violation, which is serious, but it is not outside scope.

options.text: Declining a skill within your scope
options.rationale: Declining may be a clinical judgement. It does not exceed anything.

items.explanation_md: Scope violations and protocol violations are different failures with different consequences. Both matter; only one is practising without a licence.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Why is scope confusion the most common root of AEMT disciplinary action?

options.text: Because the boundary is invisible at the bedside and only becomes clear afterwards
options.rationale: Nothing on scene stops you. The line is found in review, and by then the act is done.

options.text: Because AEMT scope changes frequently
options.rationale: It is fairly stable. The problem is knowing where it sits, not tracking changes.

options.text: Because protocols are optional
options.rationale: They are not optional.

options.text: Because states do not publish their scope
options.rationale: They publish it. It has to be read.

items.explanation_md: This is why the boundary is worth knowing cold rather than looking up: on a bad call there is no time to look it up.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: What is the standard of care used to judge your actions after a call?

options.text: What a reasonable provider of the same level would have done in the same circumstances
options.rationale: It is a comparison to a reasonable peer, not to an ideal or to hindsight.

options.text: What the best provider in the service would have done
options.rationale: The comparison is to a reasonable provider, not the best one.

options.text: What the protocol says, word for word
options.rationale: Protocol is evidence of the standard, not the whole of it.

options.text: What the outcome turned out to be
options.rationale: A bad outcome does not by itself establish a breach.

items.explanation_md: Reasonable, same level, same circumstances. Protocol is strong evidence of what reasonable looks like, which is why deviating from it needs a reason you can state.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Where would you look to find what you may do on a given call today?

options.text: Your protocol, having confirmed the skill is within your state scope
options.rationale: Protocol inside scope is the operative answer for today.

options.text: The national Scope of Practice Model alone
options.rationale: It is a model states adapt. It is not your authority.

options.text: The national certification examination blueprint
options.rationale: That describes what is tested, not what you may perform.

options.text: Whatever your partner did last shift
options.rationale: Practice is not set by precedent on the truck.

items.explanation_md: The national model shapes state law; state law sets your ceiling; protocol tells you what to do beneath it.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Put the stages of a typical emergency call in order.

options.text: Public access — someone calls for help
options.rationale: Nothing starts until the system is told.

options.text: Dispatch — the call is triaged and a resource is sent
options.rationale: Dispatch decides what goes and gives pre-arrival instructions.

options.text: Prehospital assessment and treatment
options.rationale: The crew arrives and care begins.

options.text: Transport to a capable destination
options.rationale: Care continues to a facility able to take over.

options.text: Transfer of care and definitive treatment
options.rationale: The handoff and what follows it.

items.explanation_md: Every component exists to move a patient from the moment of need to definitive care. A weak link anywhere costs the whole chain.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What is the purpose of emergency medical dispatch giving pre-arrival instructions?

options.text: Care begins before the ambulance arrives
options.rationale: Compressions or bleeding control started by a caller can decide the outcome.

options.text: It keeps the caller occupied
options.rationale: The instructions are clinical, not a distraction.

options.text: It replaces the need for a rapid response
options.rationale: It supplements it and never replaces it.

options.text: It establishes legal consent
options.rationale: Consent is a separate matter entirely.

items.explanation_md: Bystander compressions and early bleeding control are among the highest-value interventions in the whole system.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select every component that is part of an EMS system rather than an individual call.

options.text: Medical direction
options.rationale: A system component, present on every call whether or not you speak to anyone.

options.text: Continuous quality improvement
options.rationale: A system function that reviews care after the fact.

options.text: Public education and prevention
options.rationale: Reducing the calls that happen at all is a system role.

options.text: The patient’s chief complaint
options.rationale: That belongs to one call.

options.text: Your assessment findings
options.rationale: Also specific to one patient.

items.explanation_md: The system is the thing that exists between calls. Recognising that is what makes CQI and prevention make sense.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A rural service has long transport times. Which system component most directly compensates?

options.text: Air medical and mutual aid arrangements built into the response plan
options.rationale: Distance is answered by planning resources into the system in advance.

options.text: Increasing the number of protocols
options.rationale: More paper does not shorten a transport.

options.text: More frequent recertification
options.rationale: Valuable, but it does not address distance.

options.text: Reducing dispatch triage
options.rationale: That would make matters worse.

items.explanation_md: System design is how geography is answered. It is decided long before the call comes in.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Which component of the system reviews care after the call to improve it?

options.text: Continuous quality improvement
options.rationale: CQI closes the loop between what was done and what is taught next.

options.text: Medical direction
options.rationale: It authorises care; review is a distinct function, though the medical director takes part.

options.text: Dispatch
options.rationale: Dispatch sends resources.

options.text: Public access
options.rationale: That is how a call reaches the system.

items.explanation_md: Without review, a system repeats its mistakes indefinitely and never learns from what went well.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Why is an interfacility transfer still an EMS call rather than a taxi journey?

options.text: The patient is under your care throughout, at a level the sending facility specified
options.rationale: The whole point is continuing a level of care in transit.

options.text: Because it is billed the same way
options.rationale: Billing is not what makes it clinical.

options.text: Because it uses the same vehicle
options.rationale: The vehicle is incidental.

options.text: Because the patient is on a stretcher
options.rationale: A stretcher does not make a journey clinical either.

items.explanation_md: A transfer is an unbroken continuation of care. That is why the level of crew sent to one is a clinical decision.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Which part of the system does each belong to?

rows.label: Pre-arrival CPR instructions to a caller
A standing order for nebulised albuterol
A chart audit of every refusal last month
Triaging a 911 call to the right resource

items.explanation_md: Knowing which part of the system owns a problem tells you who can actually fix it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Your service cannot get a crew to a rural address within a reasonable time, repeatedly. Whose problem is that?

options.text: The system’s — it is a resource deployment question, raised through the service
options.rationale: Individual crews cannot solve coverage. It is designed, and it is changed by raising it.

options.text: The responding crew’s, for not driving faster
options.rationale: Driving faster adds risk and saves very little time.

options.text: The caller’s, for living rurally
options.rationale: Access to emergency care is not a personal failing.

options.text: Nobody’s — rural response is simply slow
options.rationale: Treating it as inevitable is how it stays unexamined.

items.explanation_md: Recognising a system problem as a system problem is the first step to it being fixed rather than absorbed.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What is the difference between online and offline medical direction?

options.text: Online is contemporaneous contact with a physician; offline is written in advance
options.rationale: Offline is your protocols and standing orders. Online is the call you make.

options.text: Online is by radio; offline is by telephone
options.rationale: Both are contemporaneous contact. The channel is not the distinction.

options.text: Online applies to emergencies; offline to transfers
options.rationale: Both apply everywhere.

options.text: Online is optional; offline is mandatory
options.rationale: Both are binding when they apply.

items.explanation_md: Offline direction is the physician’s judgement written down before the call. Online is their judgement applied to the call in front of you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A standing order covers your patient’s presentation exactly. What does that permit?

options.text: Acting immediately, without contacting a physician first
options.rationale: That is what a standing order is for — the authorisation was given in advance.

options.text: Acting only after radio contact
options.rationale: Requiring contact would defeat the purpose of the standing order.

options.text: Acting only with a paramedic present
options.rationale: A standing order is written to your level.

options.text: Acting outside your scope if the order says so
options.rationale: No order can exceed your licence.

items.explanation_md: Standing orders exist so time-critical care is not delayed by a phone call. Using one is not a shortcut.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select every situation that calls for contacting online medical direction.

options.text: The presentation does not fit any standing order you have
options.rationale: An unanticipated situation is exactly what online direction is for.

options.text: You believe a deviation from protocol is in the patient’s interest
options.rationale: Deviations need a physician’s agreement, contemporaneously.

options.text: A protocol explicitly requires physician contact before an intervention
options.rationale: Where the protocol says call, calling is the protocol.

options.text: A standing order covers the presentation exactly
options.rationale: Then the authorisation already exists.

options.text: You want a second opinion on a routine transport
options.rationale: Not a clinical need, and it occupies a line others may need.

items.explanation_md: Call when the written direction runs out, when you want to depart from it, or when it tells you to.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Online medical direction gives you an order that is outside your scope of practice. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, state why, and offer what is within your scope
options.rationale: A physician order cannot extend your licence. Saying so is part of the job.

options.text: Carry it out — a physician has assumed responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility does not transfer a licence. You would be practising outside scope.

options.text: Carry it out and document the physician’s name
options.rationale: Documenting it does not make it lawful.

options.text: Carry it out only if the patient is critical
options.rationale: Urgency does not widen scope.

items.explanation_md: This is rare, and it is worth rehearsing precisely because it is rare. The answer is the same as in 1.1: nobody can widen your scope on scene.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: What is the medical director’s role in the service?

options.text: A physician who authorises and oversees the clinical care the service provides
options.rationale: Prehospital care is delivered under their licence and their oversight.

options.text: A supervisor of day-to-day operations
options.rationale: That is an operational role, not the medical director’s.

options.text: An employee of the state EMS office
options.rationale: They are appointed by or contracted to the service.

options.text: The author of the national scope model
options.rationale: That is a national body.

items.explanation_md: Every protocol you work under is theirs. That is why departures from it are discussed with them and not decided alone.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Does each situation need online direction, or is offline direction enough?

rows.label: Nebulised bronchodilator for wheezing covered by protocol
A dose beyond the maximum the protocol states
A presentation no protocol addresses
Oxygen for a hypoxic patient

items.explanation_md: The test is simple: does written direction already cover this, exactly? If yes, act. If not, call.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Why does delaying a standing-order intervention to call medical control cause harm?

options.text: It costs time in a situation where the physician has already given the answer
options.rationale: The order exists so the delay does not happen. Calling adds risk without adding information.

options.text: It annoys the physician
options.rationale: Irrelevant to the patient.

options.text: It is a protocol violation
options.rationale: Calling unnecessarily is not usually a violation. The harm is the delay.

options.text: It transfers liability to you
options.rationale: Liability is not what makes this the wrong choice.

items.explanation_md: A standing order is a decision already made. Re-asking for it spends the minutes it was written to save.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: You receive a radio order you did not hear clearly. What do you do before acting?

options.text: Repeat it back and have it confirmed
options.rationale: Closed-loop confirmation is how a misheard order is caught before it is given.

options.text: Act on what you think you heard
options.rationale: That is how wrong drugs and wrong doses happen.

options.text: Ask your partner what they heard
options.rationale: Two people can mishear the same transmission the same way.

options.text: Record it and query afterwards
options.rationale: Afterwards is too late if it was wrong.

items.explanation_md: Read back and confirm. It costs seconds and it is the only step that catches a misheard order.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Radio contact fails and your patient needs an intervention your standing orders cover. What governs?

options.text: The standing order — it is direction, given in advance, and still in force
options.rationale: Offline direction does not depend on the radio working.

options.text: Nothing — you must wait until contact is restored
options.rationale: Waiting would withhold care the physician already authorised.

options.text: Your own judgement, unconstrained
options.rationale: You remain inside protocol and scope.

options.text: The receiving hospital’s instructions
options.rationale: They are not your medical direction.

items.explanation_md: This is the practical reason offline direction exists: it works when nothing else does.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What principle decides a destination when the nearest hospital cannot treat the problem?

options.text: Capability — go to a facility that can deliver the definitive treatment
options.rationale: A short transport to a facility that must then transfer usually costs the patient time.

options.text: Proximity, always
options.rationale: Nearest is right only when nearest is capable.

options.text: Whichever facility the family prefers
options.rationale: Preference matters and is considered, but capability comes first in a time-critical case.

options.text: Whichever has the shortest wait
options.rationale: Waiting time does not substitute for capability.

items.explanation_md: Specialty systems exist because some conditions need a capability that not every hospital has. Bypassing for capability is the point.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Sort each presentation by the specialty capability it most needs.

options.text: Unilateral weakness with a clear time of onset
options.rationale: Time-dependent stroke care needs imaging and a stroke pathway.

options.text: ST elevation on a transmitted 12-lead
options.rationale: Definitive treatment is catheterisation.

options.text: Penetrating abdominal injury with hypotension
options.rationale: That needs an operating theatre and a surgeon.

options.text: Fall from height with an open femur fracture
options.rationale: Major trauma capability.

items.explanation_md: Each specialty system exists because its treatment is time-dependent and not universally available.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: An interfacility transfer is requested at a level of care above your own. What should happen?

options.text: A crew at the required level is sent instead
options.rationale: The sending clinician specifies the level; the service must meet it.

options.text: You take it and call for help if needed
options.rationale: Accepting a transfer you cannot staff commits the patient to a gap.

options.text: You take it if the distance is short
options.rationale: Distance does not change the level of care required.

options.text: The receiving facility decides
options.rationale: The sending clinician specifies what the patient needs in transit.

items.explanation_md: Accepting a transfer above your level is a scope problem that begins before the wheels move.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select everything that should inform a destination decision.

options.text: What the patient needs and which facilities provide it
options.rationale: Capability is the first question.

options.text: Transport time to each candidate facility
options.rationale: Time is part of capability when treatment is time-dependent.

options.text: Any destination requirement in your protocol
options.rationale: Protocol may direct or restrict destinations.

options.text: Which facility your crew prefers
options.rationale: Crew preference is not a clinical input.

options.text: Which facility is least busy for you
options.rationale: Convenience to the crew is not a patient consideration.

items.explanation_md: Capability, time, protocol — and the patient’s own preference where the case is not time-critical.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A stable patient asks to go to a hospital further away where their records are. Is that reasonable?

options.text: Yes, if the patient is stable and it does not conflict with protocol
options.rationale: Continuity of care is a genuine benefit, and a stable patient may choose.

options.text: No — always transport to the nearest facility
options.rationale: Nearest is not a rule; it is a default when time matters.

options.text: No — patients may not choose a destination
options.rationale: They may, within clinical and protocol limits.

options.text: Only if the crew agrees it is convenient
options.rationale: Convenience does not enter it.

items.explanation_md: The tighter the clinical time pressure, the less room there is for preference. In a stable patient there is usually room.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Why can transporting a major trauma patient to a closer non-trauma hospital cost time overall?

options.text: The patient must then be stabilised and transferred again, adding a whole second journey
options.rationale: Two transports and an interval of waiting usually exceed the longer first transport.

options.text: Non-trauma hospitals refuse trauma patients
options.rationale: They do not refuse; they stabilise and transfer.

options.text: Ambulances are not permitted to bypass
options.rationale: Bypass for capability is normal and protocol-directed.

options.text: It costs more to bill
options.rationale: Not a clinical consideration.

items.explanation_md: The question is never "which is nearest" but "which route gets the definitive treatment soonest".
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Is proximity or capability the deciding factor?

rows.label: Uncontrolled airway you cannot manage
Suspected large-vessel stroke within the treatment window
ST elevation on the 12-lead
Cardiac arrest you cannot resuscitate en route

items.explanation_md: Capability wins for time-dependent definitive treatment. Proximity wins when the patient will not survive the extra distance.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Your protocol names a destination and the patient asks for a different one. What comes first?

options.text: Discuss it, and follow protocol where it is directive — contacting medical control if it is genuinely contested
options.rationale: Protocol governs, but a contested destination is exactly what medical control is for.

options.text: The patient’s preference, always
options.rationale: Preference does not override a directive protocol.

options.text: The crew’s decision, without discussion
options.rationale: Deciding without discussing it is how complaints begin.

options.text: The nearest facility, regardless
options.rationale: That answers neither the protocol nor the patient.

items.explanation_md: Most destination disputes dissolve once the reason is explained. The ones that do not are a medical control call.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What is continuous quality improvement meant to do?

options.text: Find and fix the system causes of recurring problems
options.rationale: CQI looks for the pattern behind the incident, and changes the system.

options.text: Identify individuals to discipline
options.rationale: A process that finds people to blame stops receiving honest reports, and then stops working.

options.text: Satisfy a documentation requirement
options.rationale: It produces documentation; that is not its purpose.

options.text: Rank crews against each other
options.rationale: Ranking does not identify causes.

items.explanation_md: A CQI process that people fear is a CQI process that stops being told anything, and it is then worse than none.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A practice has been standard for thirty years. What does that establish about whether it works?

options.text: Very little — longevity is not evidence of benefit
options.rationale: Several long-standing EMS practices have turned out to lack evidence of benefit, and some carried harm.

options.text: That it works, or it would have been abandoned
options.rationale: Practices persist for many reasons other than efficacy.

options.text: That it is safe
options.rationale: Duration says nothing about harm either.

options.text: That it is required by law
options.rationale: Custom is not law.

items.explanation_md: This is worth holding onto. Later in this series you will meet two practices the textbook teaches and the current evidence does not support.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select every question worth asking about a claimed practice improvement.

options.text: What evidence supports it, and how strong is that evidence?
options.rationale: The first question, and the one most often skipped.

options.text: What outcome was actually measured?
options.rationale: A change in a surrogate measure is not a change in survival.

options.text: Who benefits if it is adopted?
options.rationale: Worth knowing, particularly where a product is involved.

options.text: How long has it been taught?
options.rationale: Longevity is not evidence, which is the point of this block.

options.text: Whether other services do it
options.rationale: Common practice is not the same as supported practice.

items.explanation_md: Evidence, outcome, interest. Three questions that separate a real improvement from a confident one.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Your service changes a protocol because of a new study. What should the change rest on?

options.text: The medical director’s appraisal of the evidence against current practice
options.rationale: A single study is an input to a judgement, not an instruction.

options.text: The study alone, immediately
options.rationale: One study rarely overturns a practice by itself.

options.text: Whether the study agrees with existing practice
options.rationale: That reasoning would prevent any change ever.

options.text: How widely the study was reported
options.rationale: Coverage is not quality.

items.explanation_md: The medical director owns the protocol precisely so evidence is appraised rather than adopted on headline.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: How much weight does each piece of support carry?

rows.label: Several randomised trials agreeing on a patient outcome
A manufacturer’s claim about their own device
"We have always done it this way"
A systematic review of many studies

items.explanation_md: Evidence literacy is a clinical skill. It is what lets you tell an improvement from a fashion.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: You make an error on a call that causes no harm. What should you do?

options.text: Report it, so the system can find out why it was possible
options.rationale: Near misses are the cheapest information a system ever gets.

options.text: Say nothing, since nobody was hurt
options.rationale: The next occurrence may not be harmless, and nothing will have changed.

options.text: Tell your partner only
options.rationale: It does not reach anyone who can change the system.

options.text: Correct the record to remove it
options.rationale: Altering a record to conceal an error is a separate and far more serious problem.

items.explanation_md: A system only learns from what it is told. The error that harms nobody is the one you most want reported.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A device is promoted on a study showing it improves a number on the monitor. What limits that evidence?

options.text: It measured a surrogate, not an outcome that matters to the patient
options.rationale: A better waveform is not the same as a patient who survives or recovers function.

options.text: A single study is never worth reading
options.rationale: One study is an input. The problem here is what it measured, not that there is one.

options.text: Monitors are unreliable
options.rationale: The measurement may be perfectly accurate and still be the wrong thing to measure.

options.text: Devices cannot be studied properly
options.rationale: They can be, and some are, against survival and function.

items.explanation_md: Surrogate outcomes are the most common way a weak claim looks strong. Ask what was measured before you ask how large the effect was.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What makes a chart audit useful to a service?

options.text: It shows patterns across many calls that no single crew could see
options.rationale: Aggregate review finds what individual experience cannot.

options.text: It identifies the weakest provider
options.rationale: That is not what aggregate data is good at, and chasing it poisons reporting.

options.text: It satisfies the billing department
options.rationale: Billing review is a separate exercise.

options.text: It proves care was correct
options.rationale: It examines care; it does not certify it.

items.explanation_md: One crew sees their own calls. The audit sees all of them, which is the only way a pattern becomes visible.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: What is mobile integrated healthcare?

options.text: Using EMS resources to deliver planned care outside emergency response
options.rationale: Follow-up visits, chronic disease support, navigation to the right service.

options.text: A faster form of emergency response
options.rationale: It is not about response speed at all.

options.text: A transport service for non-emergency patients
options.rationale: Transport is often exactly what MIH avoids.

options.text: A paramedic working in a hospital
options.rationale: That is a different role.

items.explanation_md: MIH and community paramedicine treat EMS as a healthcare resource that happens to be mobile, rather than only a response system.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Select the attributes most often named as professional conduct in EMS.

options.text: Integrity — recording what happened, including your own errors
options.rationale: The record is only useful if it is true.

options.text: Respect — for patients, families and other services
options.rationale: Named in every professional standard.

options.text: Self-motivation — maintaining competence without being told
options.rationale: Skills decay whether or not anyone checks.

options.text: Deference — never questioning an order
options.rationale: Questioning an unsafe order is part of the job, as 1.4 showed.

options.text: Speed above all
options.rationale: Speed that adds risk is not professionalism.

items.explanation_md: These are what keeps a licence, and more importantly what makes a crew someone a patient can trust.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: You realise mid-shift that you have forgotten part of a skill you rarely use. What is the professional response?

options.text: Say so, and arrange to refresh it
options.rationale: Competence maintained honestly is what the attribute actually means.

options.text: Avoid calls where it might be needed
options.rationale: You cannot choose your calls, and the gap remains.

options.text: Look it up if it comes up
options.rationale: Reading a procedure for the first time at the bedside is not competence.

options.text: Assume it will return under pressure
options.rationale: Skills degrade, and pressure is when they degrade most.

items.explanation_md: Rarely used skills decay fastest. Saying so is the professional act, not the embarrassing one.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A frequent caller uses the ambulance for problems better met elsewhere. What does an MIH approach offer?

options.text: A planned route to the service that actually addresses the underlying need
options.rationale: MIH exists for exactly this pattern.

options.text: A way to refuse the calls
options.rationale: Refusal is not a clinical solution and rarely lawful.

options.text: Transport to a different hospital
options.rationale: A different door does not change the unmet need.

options.text: Nothing — it is a social problem
options.rationale: Repeat use of emergency services is a healthcare problem with a healthcare answer.

items.explanation_md: Repeat callers are usually a signal that a need is unmet somewhere else in the system.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Is each action consistent with professional conduct?

rows.label: Recording a vital sign you did not take
Telling the receiving nurse about your own error
Discussing a recognisable patient on social media
Refreshing a skill you have not used in a year

items.explanation_md: Two of these end careers. Both involve the record or the patient’s privacy, which Chapter 3 takes up in detail.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Why is appearance and manner treated as a clinical matter rather than a cosmetic one?

options.text: A patient who does not trust you withholds information you need
options.rationale: History is the bulk of your assessment, and it depends on being told the truth.

options.text: It is required by uniform policy
options.rationale: Policy exists, but that is not the clinical reason.

options.text: It affects billing
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: It determines scope
options.rationale: Scope is set by law.

items.explanation_md: Trust is an assessment tool. A frightened or unconvinced patient tells you less, and you decide with less.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Your service starts an MIH programme. Which result would best show it is working?

options.text: Enrolled patients call 911 less because the underlying need is being met elsewhere
options.rationale: Needs met rather than patients moved is the measure the model is built around.

options.text: The programme enrols more patients each month
options.rationale: Enrolment is activity. It says nothing about whether anyone is better off.

options.text: Transports per shift increase
options.rationale: MIH usually reduces transports; more of them is not the aim.

options.text: Response times fall
options.rationale: A response-time change is not what this model sets out to produce.

items.explanation_md: This is 1.6 applied to your own service: ask what was actually measured, and whether it is the thing you care about.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Community paramedicine most often aims to do what?

options.text: Meet a patient’s need without an emergency department visit where that is appropriate
options.rationale: Often through follow-up, assessment at home, or navigation to another service.

options.text: Increase ambulance transports
options.rationale: It usually reduces them.

options.text: Replace primary care
options.rationale: It connects to primary care rather than replacing it.

options.text: Expand paramedic scope of practice
options.rationale: It is a deployment model, not a scope change.

items.explanation_md: The measure of success is usually a need met, not a patient moved.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

stimulus.text:
0410. You and your EMT partner are dispatched to a 58-year-old man with chest pain, thirty-five minutes from the nearest hospital. That hospital has an emergency department but no catheterisation laboratory. A PCI centre is fifty-five minutes away.

He is pale and sweating. Your 12-lead shows clear ST elevation. Your protocol has a standing order for aspirin, and directs transport to a PCI centre for ST elevation. Your partner says the closer hospital is safer because it is closer.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: The standing order covers aspirin. What do you do about contacting medical control first?

options.text: Give it now — the authorisation was given in advance
options.rationale: That is what a standing order is. Calling would spend time it exists to save.

options.text: Call for permission before giving it
options.rationale: It is already permitted. The call adds delay and no information.

options.text: Wait until you have chosen a destination
options.rationale: The two decisions are independent.

options.text: Ask the receiving hospital
options.rationale: They are not your medical direction.

items.explanation_md: Offline direction is a decision already made. Acting on it is the correct use of it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Your partner argues for the closer hospital. What is the strongest counter?

options.text: The closer hospital cannot deliver the definitive treatment, so he would be transferred again
options.rationale: Two journeys and a wait between them usually exceed the extra twenty minutes.

options.text: Protocol says so, so there is nothing to discuss
options.rationale: True, but it does not answer the clinical question and does not persuade.

options.text: The PCI centre is better staffed overall
options.rationale: The relevant difference is the catheterisation laboratory, not general staffing.

options.text: The patient will prefer it
options.rationale: You have not asked him, and this is time-critical.

items.explanation_md: The real question is which route reaches the definitive treatment soonest, not which door is nearest.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Which type of medical direction is directing your destination here?

options.text: Offline — the protocol was written in advance
options.rationale: A destination protocol is written direction.

options.text: Online — because you may radio the hospital
options.rationale: Notifying a hospital is not the same as receiving direction from a physician.

options.text: Neither — destination is a crew decision
options.rationale: Where protocol directs, it governs.

options.text: Both equally
options.rationale: Only the written protocol is directing you at this point.

items.explanation_md: Most of what you do on a call runs on offline direction. Online is the exception, not the norm.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Which facts here make this a capability decision rather than a proximity one?

options.text: ST elevation, whose definitive treatment is catheterisation
options.rationale: The treatment he needs exists in only one of the two facilities.

options.text: The nearer hospital has no catheterisation laboratory
options.rationale: That is the capability gap.

options.text: The protocol directs PCI centre transport for ST elevation
options.rationale: The system has already made this decision.

options.text: It is 0410
options.rationale: The hour does not change what he needs.

options.text: Your partner disagrees
options.rationale: A disagreement to resolve, not a clinical fact.

items.explanation_md: Three facts, all pointing the same way. Recognising which facts are decisive is most of clinical judgement.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: En route he becomes unresponsive and you cannot manage his airway with what you carry. Does the destination change?

options.text: Yes — an airway you cannot manage makes the nearest facility the right one now
options.rationale: Capability wins until the patient will not survive the distance. Then proximity wins.

options.text: No — the protocol named a PCI centre
options.rationale: Protocol assumes a patient who survives the journey.

options.text: No — changing destination is never permitted
options.rationale: It is, when the clinical picture changes.

options.text: Only if medical control agrees first
options.rationale: Advise them, but do not withhold the diversion waiting for a reply.

items.explanation_md: The rule from 1.5 has both halves: capability for time-dependent treatment, proximity when the patient will not survive the extra distance.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: A physician on the radio orders a drug outside your AEMT scope. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, say why, and offer what is within your scope
options.rationale: Nobody on a radio can extend your licence.

options.text: Give it — the physician has taken responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility does not transfer a licence to you.

options.text: Give it and document the order carefully
options.rationale: Careful documentation of an unlawful act does not help.

options.text: Have your EMT partner give it
options.rationale: It is further outside their scope than yours.

items.explanation_md: The same answer as 1.1 and 1.4, tested here under pressure, because that is where it is actually hard.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Which part of the system will examine this call afterwards, and to what end?

options.text: Continuous quality improvement, looking for what the system can change
options.rationale: Aggregate review looks for causes, not culprits.

options.text: Medical direction, to decide discipline
options.rationale: Discipline is a separate process, and a CQI system built on it stops being told anything.

options.text: Dispatch, to review the address
options.rationale: Not the function.

options.text: Nobody — the call went well
options.rationale: Calls that go well are exactly the ones worth understanding.

items.explanation_md: A long transport for capability is a system question: is the coverage right, and does the protocol still fit the geography?
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.

items.stem: Which skills on this call were within your AEMT scope?

options.text: IV access and the aspirin your protocol authorises
options.rationale: Both sit within the AEMT scope and within your protocol.

options.text: Interpreting the 12-lead as a basis for treatment decisions
options.rationale: Rhythm and 12-lead interpretation is paramedic-level; transmitting it is different from acting on your own reading.

options.text: Needle decompression if his chest had been involved
options.rationale: Paramedic-level.

options.text: Endotracheal intubation for the airway
options.rationale: Above AEMT scope.

items.explanation_md: Acquiring and transmitting a 12-lead is a task; interpreting it as the basis for treatment is a scope question.
items.source_ref: National EMS Scope of Practice Model (NHTSA, 2019; 2021 update) — AEMT.

items.stem: Reviewing this call, which decisions would you expect to defend and be able to?

options.text: Giving aspirin on the standing order without calling
options.rationale: Written direction covered it exactly.

options.text: Bypassing the nearer hospital for the PCI centre
options.rationale: Protocol-directed and clinically reasoned.

options.text: Diverting when the airway failed
options.rationale: A change in the clinical picture changed the right answer.

options.text: Declining the out-of-scope order
options.rationale: Correct, and the only lawful option.

options.text: Deferring to your partner’s preference for the closer hospital
options.rationale: That would have been the one decision you could not defend.

items.explanation_md: Four defensible decisions and one that would not have been. Being able to say why afterwards is what the whole chapter is for.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: EMS Systems.
